11 Great Photography Podcasts You Should Know

Looking for the best photography podcasts? These 11 standout shows bring you closer to the photographers, ideas and stories shaping the medium today.

It’s no exaggeration to say that we are living in a time of great information overload. Bitesize hot takes, floating fragments of information and easily-digestible summaries jostle for attention on our screens. This is a problem when it comes to talking about photography. An unruly medium, in flux since its birth, continuing to surprise us as it shapeshifts through this visually-stimulating, post-truth world where even our understanding of reality has come under scrutiny… There’s simply nothing simple about it. Enter the world of photography podcasts!

“It’s not this; it’s this.” When Chat GPT is making the world sound more and more like it’s being narrated by the same person, the human voice—along with all the digressions, emotions and embodied knowledge that it holds and its ability to be in true dialogue with another—starts to feel very powerful.

But where to start? What can audio contribute to a visual medium? The answer is a lot. From interviews with artists to historical reflections on the artists that have shaped the medium to in-depth discussions about ethics via reports from festivals and gatherings across the world, there is something out there for everyone.

Community has always been an incredibly vital part of what can often feel like a solitary craft. After all, photography is a relational artform. But the question of access can often be a complicated one. For the past 10 years, podcasts about photography have mushroomed with many hosts focusing on what they’d like to hear. What was once a relatively empty landscape has now grown from the ground up into an extensive and responsive terrain that reflects photography’s lively global network—and opens the door to it no matter where you are based. Mostly free, or with a small subscription fee to help support independent creators, they give us unprecedented access to some of the industry’s most interesting voices while celebrating and nurturing the communal aspect of photography.

Surprisingly, a medium that hinges on the act of speaking—and the invitation to listen—works wonders for one that is silent and relies on looking. Occurring off-screen (sometimes with video options for those who like to watch along) there is space for the mind to wander and listen closely. For those ‘on air,’ the unpredictable nature of conversation allows room for the intimacies, intricacies and contradictions that photography produces to remain alive. In this period of great change and turmoil, the podcast space feels almost like a salon where interesting people in the know get together to tackle the big questions as they arise. And what a joy it is to listen along.

We’ve listened to lots of photography podcasts. Here is our curated list of what’s playing on our headphones.

[](https://shows.acast.com/themessytruth)

> The Messy Truth

Hosted by British photo director, writer and editor Gem Fletcher, The Messy Truth is focused on the world of contemporary photography—and the changes it’s undergoing. Fletcher is a curious guide whose questions are those of a passionate insider with their finger on the medium’s pulse, grounded in many years of experience supporting artists. Driven by finding out “what makes artists tick,” discussions circle around themes like truth, audience, consent, working in a “two-screen” image culture, misinformation, balancing art and commerce to reflect the image world as it is, in all its mess. Guests are varied, including Carolyn Drake and Andres Gonzalez, Jack Davison, curator Vince Aletti and photo editor Kathy Ryan. To mark her 100th episode, Fletcher collaborated with ICP to host an invaluable one day salon called Between Two Worlds, as “an attempt to describe the feeling of existing in two image worlds, the one we think we know, and the new one emerging.”

Listen if you’re curious about the issues affecting photography today and where we might be headed tomorrow.

[](https://shows.acast.com/magic-hour)

> The Magic Hour

This podcast grew out of Magic Hour Press, an independent publisher based between Montreal and New York run by Jordan Weitzman. As a consequence, it starts from an acute understanding of photography as a language and an interest in how image and text speak to one another, explored through a well-curated list of singular artists, editors and publishers. The archive of 61 episodes is full of different approaches to the magic of editing, featuring many charmers. Duane Michals, the show’s first ever guest, sets the tone by talking about his “prose portraits.” There’s Jason Fulford talking about balancing logic and emotion and Dayanita Singh recounting how she once laid out an entire photobook exhibition in her hotel room. Many of the conversations offer an intimate look into the artists’ early career moves—a refreshing insight into the winding, idiosyncratic paths a life in photography may lead you if you take matters into your own hands.

Listen for inspiration from some greats on how to nurture creativity and chart your own course through photography.

[](https://righteyedominant.buzzsprout.com/)

> Right Eye Dominant

In the trailer for the podcast, Nick Tauro Jr. explains his passion for the longevity of photographs—from prints to a birthday card sent to your grandma to a zine or a self-published book. This love for the lasting nature of photography and its materiality underlies the themes explored in Right Eye Dominant. In our digital society of “1s and 0s on screens,” the podcast pays attention to the past as well as the present. Naming Robert Frank as the “patron saint” of the podcast (and subject of its 100th episode), it features deep dives into the work of important historical figures such as Julia Margaret Cameron, Daido Moriyama and Peter Hujar with Tauro Jr. often inviting experts in to bring these artists to life. There are also essayistic episodes on themes such as Route 66, death and photography and cameraless work, as well as interviews with contemporary photographers like Anastasia Samoylova and Jeff Cowen.

This cabinet of curiosities is for fans of analog photography and those who want to know more about the history of the medium.

> Emulsions Podcast

[](https://emulsionspodcast.buzzsprout.com/)

Emulsions, hosted by Stephen K. Schuster and Hollis Monk Thayer, is also one for analog film lovers with an interesting twist. Grounded in New York City—and more specifically the scene of photographers working with film towards the edge of the millennium—the pair often discuss analog’s proliferation in the digital world. There’s an episode on the Tumblr era and Instagram as well as hands-on, in-depth conversations about testing and experimenting with developing film at home. They talk about craft to a range of guests from Stephen Shore and Daniel Arnold to Alfred Bradshaw, who shares some indispensable technical darkroom wisdom that comes from developing a quarter million images in the past eight years. In addition to deep dives into the work of historical artists such as Vivien Maier, Gordon Parks and William Eggleston, they also explore topics like the benefits of working with film, shooting with the seasons and thinking in black and white.

Listen if you’re interested in meeting New York’s lively photo community and picking up some tips on your analog practice.

[](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/light-work-podcast/id1504144958)

> Light Work Podcast

You might already be familiar with Light Work, an artist-run non-profit in Syracuse, New York that hosts residencies, makes publications and exhibitions and runs a community lab in support of artists working in photography and media. Its podcast hands the mic directly to the artists it works with to talk briefly—each one usually runs under 10 minutes—about their process and practice. These mini-pods offer a great, more intimate alternative to the written artist statement, which is a notoriously difficult form to pull off in an interesting way, as well as introducing us to a diverse bunch of artists working today.

Listen if you’re short on time, or struggle with longer formats, and want to make some new discoveries.[](https://www.eyeshotstreetphotography.com/conversations/?query-105-page=3)

> Eyeshot 50MM

Describing itself as a “slow read, not a hot take,” the audio branch of Italian street and documentary photography publisher Eyeshot certainly revolves around questions rather than answers. What kind of agency do we have at this moment of great technological change? How can photographers keep integrity in the age of AI? What happens when you land in a new place to work? In a series of in-depth interviews with a varied list of photographers, thinkers, editors and writers, host Lucrezia Bonarota guides her guests into exploring both the ethical and the practical concerns that shape the documentary practice today—as well as its unpredictable future. The result informs listeners on workflow and process as well as chewing on big topics head-on like the status of truth, the importance of image literacy and what words bring to pictures.

Check out if you’re interested in the big questions or are curious about the “on the ground” experience of being a documentary photographer navigating an increasingly complicated terrain.

> Real Photo Show

Host Michael Choven-Dalton founded Real Photo Show with the aim of creating a space for “photographers to build community among photographers.” With this in mind, the show focuses on the origins and inspirations of photo work but also teaching, learning, distribution and other facets of the industry. As well as artists like Raymond Meeks and Vanessa Winship, Choven-Dalton speaks to interesting projects that support them, such as founders of the residency space the Wassaic Project, NY, or Jackie Battenfield author of a book called The Artist’s Guide: How to Make a Living Doing What You Love. For some time now, the podcast has been affiliated with, and present, at a photobook retreat called Chico Review. The episodes recorded in Montana are a valuable resource, inviting us into the conversations that take place at such an event.

Listen for photobook inspiration and to travel to events you might not be attending otherwise.

[](https://asmallvoicepodcast.com/)

> A Small Voice

Photographer Ben Smith started the podcast he wanted to listen to back in 2015: one that sounds like an interesting chat between friends about work. The archive is now at around 300 episodes. Smith asks the questions he is curious about, which make for natural conversations that touch on both the content of people’s work and practice, how they make a living and the state of the industry. If you don’t have the funds or energy to visit fairs and festivals, the podcast covers events such as Paris Photo, BoP Festival in Bristol and Photo London widening their accessibility and providing an energetic snapshot of what’s happening on the ground. A special episode about the Netherlands Foto Museum extends the principle to institutions too, as Smith tours the space interviewing the staff as he goes.

Listen if you want to get to know the photo community, making some trips along the way, in a casual setting.

> PhotoWork Foundation

[](https://photowork.foundation/episodes/)

Hosted by gallerist-turned photography advisor, editor and educator Sasha Wolf, PhotoWorks is billed as the “talky, touchy, feely” version of her book which interviews 40 photographers about their practice and process. A “recovering artist,” Wolf makes for a great confidante, asking all the right questions shaped by her experience of having been intimately involved in the creative process of many of her interviewees. The podcast has a strong editorial vision of wanting to share and capture the knowledge arising from the conversations Wolf was having with the artists she represents—its success confirmed in the 100th episode by a listener calling in to thank her for the “education” it had provided them with. As well as individual interviews, Wolf has a knack for bringing interesting people into dialogue to talk about shared themes.

Listen if you’re feeling adrift and looking to learn that there is no “right” way to live and work as an artist while getting inspired along the way.

> The Photobook

[](https://open.spotify.com/show/1XqF0kfl0TRta5oO4BBH95)

Hosted by New Delhi-based photographer Priyanka Chharia, this show started with a 10-episode first season that captures the journey of a photobook from conception to reality. Since, it has widened the adventure to include conversations with bookmakers, curators and publishers from all over the world. Positioning the book as a “portable portal” for connection, encounters and exchange, the podcast does a great job of shining light on the strong community at the heart of the photobook world. In addition to covering the art of “thinking in series” rather than single images and not being too precious about making a dummy, Chharia chooses guests that are also navigating what happens after a book is made to talk about distribution and audience. How can photobooks create informal spaces of friendship and care?

This one’s for you if you’re interested in the social possibilities of the photobook beyond its form and getting some advice from photobook experts.

> The Photo Ethics Podcast

Dedicated to nurturing ethical literacy in photography, the Photo Ethics Centre runs courses and workshops that research and bring awareness to the impact imagemakers have on the world. But what exactly are ethics? Hosted by Dr. Savannah Dodd, these podcast interviews explore that question through the work of many different practitioners, asking what the word means to them and how they enact it. Themes like collaboration, co-authorship, agency, sustainability, inclusivity and responsibility are discussed, making the conversations a wonderful and inspiring educational resource—one episode even distills many different conversations into eight lessons. The call is to become aware of your assumptions, be ready to make mistakes and, above all, always stay open to learning in order to keep your practice responsive. As guest writer and professor Fred Ritchin, who draws on “half a century of knowledge” dealing with images, puts it, it’s about thinking past the photography bubble to consider how your images might contribute to making the world a better place.

An important resource for anyone and everyone thinking about and making photographs today.

Alex Yudzon’s “5 Garfield Avenue” Turns Suburban America into a Horror Story

Created during a brief relocation from the New York City, displacement and domestic unease haunt the photographs in Alex Yudzon’s monochrome portrait of a house in rural Connecticut.

_Photographs by Alex Yudzon

Essay by Janelle Lynch_

[](javascript:;)

Alex Yudzon’s “5 Garfield Avenue” Turns Suburban America into a Horror Story

Created during a brief relocation from the New York City, displacement and domestic unease haunt the photographs in Alex Yudzon’s monochrome portrait of a house in rural Connecticut.

The artist Alex Yudzon’s relocation with his wife and one year-old daughter from a Brooklyn apartment to a rural Connecticut house was intended to be a respite from urban life. It would provide a slower pace, more space, and, in the nine months Yudzon and his family endured there, something unanticipated: materials, inspiration, and a setting in which to make photographs. Thirty-five of the black and white images make up 5 Garfield Avenue, Yudzon’s second monograph, which he self-published this year.

On the day of his family’s arrival, access to their new street was restricted due to a gas line rupture. Other omens soon appeared: a basement flood, faulty appliances, and a trove of abandoned boxes in the attic. An artist with an extraordinary imagination, as evidenced in Yudzon’s first monograph, A Room for a Night, published by Radius Books in 2023, he turned his new home into a working studio. From the front porch, the basement, the backyard, he created ephemeral site-specific installations and exalted the ordinary.

Basement (Figure) © Alex Yudzon[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/alex-yudzon-alex-yudzon-s-5-garfield-avenue-turns-suburban-america-into-a-horror-story#)

Yudzon was trained as a painter and constructs his images with rigorous attention to the elements of art—line, space, shape, form, texture—and the principles of design—balance, repetition, contrast, and unity. Conceptually, he draws from a range of interdisciplinary artists—John Baldessari, George Perec, Sophie Calle, and David Lynch. For more than a decade now, he has used photography as his primary medium to transform his ideas through play, spontaneity, and chance into precisely executed works of art. Cinema and his childhood experiences are, however, equally fundamental to the eerie and humorous photographs in 5 Garfield Avenue.

Midnight’s Child © Alex Yudzon

In 1985, during a peak escalation in the Cold War, eight year-old Yudzon emigrated from Moscow to the suburbs of Washington, D.C. with his parents and brother. His first memory in his new homeland is waking up in a hotel room decorated in hues of mustard yellow and brown—carpet, curtains, walls—all lit by dim light. A host would pick up Yudzon and his family later that day, but for the hours until then, in this liminal foreign space, he absorbed a deep sense of displacement.

Sidewalk with Water © Alex Yudzon[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/alex-yudzon-alex-yudzon-s-5-garfield-avenue-turns-suburban-america-into-a-horror-story#)

Once in elementary school, the artist was bullied by peers because of his Soviet origins. In his social isolation, he turned to television and became enthralled by horror films, a genre suppressed in Soviet cinema until the relaxation of censorship, including Friday the 13th, A Nightmare on Elm Street, and The Amityville Horror. About these experiences, Yudzon says: “The atmosphere of dread permeating these films mirrored my emotional reality, and I absorbed every grisly drop of blood with the wide-eyed shock of a deer in headlights. Looking back now, I realize that part of my fascination was that I identified with both the victims and the perpetrators—a connection that continues to render these films as ambivalent touchstones of my early youth.”

Encore © Alex Yudzon[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/alex-yudzon-alex-yudzon-s-5-garfield-avenue-turns-suburban-america-into-a-horror-story#)

Accompanied by a short story Yudzon authored, the images in 5 Garfield Avenue evoke the fictional world of horror and suspense while examining themes of displacement, domestic uncertainty, and exile.

Basement Figure, a vertical image, shows Yudzon’s wall-size silhouette created by hundreds of tiny torn white pieces of artist tape adhered to a wood-paneled wall. Horizontal lines surround and disrupt it. Precisely lit, the flat mosaic figure shines behind dozens of black strips hanging in the foreground. This photograph hews more toward the realm of alternate reality than horror. Similarly, Bouncy Castle is a horizontal image made from a distant wide angle of what appears to be a colossal inflatable castle soaring above a diagonal line of pine trees. In an uncanny juxtaposition, the fortress’ tower tops echo nature’s forms in the foreground and in two distant twin trees.

Bouncy Castle 2 © Alex Yudzon[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/alex-yudzon-alex-yudzon-s-5-garfield-avenue-turns-suburban-america-into-a-horror-story#)

In other images, the influence of the horror genre is more palpable. Encore, a vertical image shows two walls meeting in the center, triangles of different values and textures at the top and bottom of the frame, and a rack of hooks across the center. Hanging from the fixtures are gloves, one on each side, and above them are abstract shadows cast by blazing artificial light. Trees in Snow, a horizontal image, shows a snowy field marked by tire tracks that lead to and from barren woods fading in fog. On the following page, Car with Tree, also a horizontal, shows a partially covered car parked on a late autumn lawn between a tree and a dilapidating garage. A window is broken. Signs of abandonment abound.

In the end, it was nature that drove Yudzon and his family back to Brooklyn. A pregnant female skunk had taken up residence under the mudroom’s subfloor. State animal welfare regulations forbade the animal’s removal. Homeopathic remedies did not weaken the pungent order. Less than a month later, Yudzon and his family left Garfield Avenue.

The Global Guide to Photobook Fairs: 70+ Events Around the World

From major international festivals to independent publishing gatherings, discover more than 70 photobook fairs connecting photographers, publishers, collectors and book lovers worldwide.

_Compiled by LensCulture

Text by Magali Duzant_

[](javascript:;)

The Global Guide to Photobook Fairs: 70+ Events Around the World

From major international festivals to independent publishing gatherings, discover more than 70 photobook fairs connecting photographers, publishers, collectors and book lovers worldwide.

Books are still big—no matter how many times the death of the publishing industry has been proclaimed. And of course, the term ‘book’ is broad. Over the last few decades, artists’ books—that slippery category ranging from the handmade to glossy monographs to zines—have proliferated. None more so than photobooks. They are bound in coil or wire, stapled, sewn, or glued, sheathed in cloth or paper, table-sized or tiny. Order them online, buy them at a gallery, pop into a bookstore, peruse the shelves at the library. Or, for the most dizzying, overwhelming immersion, head to an art book fair.

At Photobook Mania in Bologna, Italy. Photobook fairs often offer great opportunities to meet the artists and authors directly during book signings and public talks. Many authors hang out at a publisher’s stand to talk with people who are browsing the books. © Photobook Mania[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-the-global-guide-to-photobook-fairs-70-events-around-the-world#)

Art book fairs and festivals are everywhere, filling rooms, tents, even boats with tables of books, zines, prints, and more (you could potentially outfit yourself from head to toe at a fair—take your pick from caps, totes, tees, and even socks). These events come in many flavors, shapes, and sizes. Some require timed tickets and others have lines down the block. There are photography-only events and zinefests, omnibus fairs drawing in thousands of visitors, and institutional ones accompanying exhibitions or conferences. They are the largest driver of engagement with photography publications, an increasingly important means of distribution, and often a pretty darn good time. But first, like flipping through a book, let’s start at the beginning.

At Photobook Mania in Bologna. Photobooks offer the rare chance to read and flick through books on the spot and make new discoveries. © Photobook Mania[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-the-global-guide-to-photobook-fairs-70-events-around-the-world#)

The book fair model in the traditional publishing industry skews corporate, with huge global events where titles are bought and sold alongside licensing rights and contract negotiations. The art book fair scene began as a counter to this; an independent, grassroots movement started by working artists themselves. This year marks the 20th anniversary of one of the first fairs of its kind (and the 50th anniversary of the institution that runs it).

Exterior view of the NY Art Book Fair—a staple event in the city’s cultural agenda. © Ally Caple[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-the-global-guide-to-photobook-fairs-70-events-around-the-world#)

In 2006, AA Bronson, the then director of Printed Matter, the famed artists’ book store in New York City, launched the inaugural New York Art Book Fair. The idea began as a way to support the distribution and understanding of artists’ books by providing a chance for artists and publishers to engage with the public, their peers, and new audiences. The NYABF’s first outing featured 70 exhibitors; recent iterations have held over 300, with publishers, artists, and collectives from across the world.

At the CPW Photobook and Zine Fair. As well as visiting all the stores you already know, fairs are packed with great independent publishers to discover. © CPW Photobook and Zine Fair[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-the-global-guide-to-photobook-fairs-70-events-around-the-world#)

In 2009, the Tokyo Art Book Fair was inaugurated, followed in 2010 by Offprint, which hosts fairs in Paris and London during photo industry events. Whether through dedicated photo publisher rooms or exhibition opportunities, photography and photobooks have been a foundational part of these fairs since the beginning. Art Basel hosts a book fair, as does Les Rencontres d’Arles, AIPAD (the Association of International Photography Art Dealers), Paris Photo, and Photo London all have photobook sections. Festivals both big and small from Images Vevey and PhMuseum Days to Philadelphia’s 20/20 Photo Festival feature book events as well.

At the CPW Photobook and Zine Fair. Some photobook fairs invite visitors to get creative too with a program of workshops and participatory events. © CPW Photobook and Zine Fair[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-the-global-guide-to-photobook-fairs-70-events-around-the-world#)

Many publishers time their new releases to coincide with fairs, which present the opportunity to program book signings and talks, to submit books to awards, and to meet with distributors and collectors. Fairs are a fantastic resource for photographers—giving an overview of the publishing scene, gathering artists, editors, curators, collectors, and designers, and providing a platform for sales and visibility as well as conversation and connection. The big names are there, from Aperture to Mack, as are smaller, experimental presses.

Many fairs host lectures, workshops, and exhibitions. At this year’s ICP Photobook Fest, one could peruse “Photo-based Books from the Collections of Center for Book Arts selected by Christian Patterson” or view the group show Twin Cities: Held Together presented by the Magnum Foundation. The shortlist for the Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards will be on view in the Grand Palais during Paris Photo and bookmaking workshops are on offer at Arles. At some fairs, industry hours are set aside, inviting institutional librarians, bookstore buyers, and collectors a quieter window to browse and familiarize themselves with new work.

At the LA Art Book Fair. Publishers are a great resource when it comes to finally making a choice, always on hand to chat about their new titles and offer advice. © Aleksey Kondratyev

Perhaps the most rewarding aspect of the fair scene is community. The photography world gathers together, to launch titles and look at new work, catch up and share ideas. You might meet the artist behind your favorite publication, listen in on a discussion of alternative distribution methods, or find a collective expanding the realm of photobook possibilities, hell you might even meet a future collaborator (reader, a fair is where I met the lovely bookstore owner I ended up marrying). Whether you’re looking for design inspiration, your new favorite title, or researching publishers, the world of book fairs beckons.

— Magali Duzant

Nazraeli Press: Interview with Photobook Publisher Chris Pichler

Nazraeli Press founder Chris Pichler reflects on four decades of publishing, the enduring power of photobooks, and what makes a project worthy of becoming a book.

Interview with Chris Pichler by Jim Casper

[](javascript:;)

Nazraeli Press: Interview with Photobook Publisher Chris Pichler

Nazraeli Press founder Chris Pichler reflects on four decades of publishing, the enduring power of photobooks, and what makes a project worthy of becoming a book.

![Image 5 Chris Pichler](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/chris-pichler-nazraeli-press-interview-with-photobook-publisher-chris-pichler)

The inaugural LensCulture Photobook Prize offers one photographer the opportunity to transform an unpublished project into a beautifully designed, professionally printed, and internationally distributed photobook — fully funded. In partnership with Nazraeli Press, the winning project will be designed, produced, and distributed worldwide. Additional prizes go to 5 Shortlisted and 10 Finalist photographers.

For this interview, LensCulture’s Jim Casper spoke with Chris Pichler, the founder and director of Nazraeli Press, who has published more than 800 photobooks and art books over the past 38 years.

Jim Casper: Thanks for taking the time for this conversation, and thanks for agreeing to be the publisher for the inaugural LensCulture Photobook Prize. It’s a very exciting new venture.

Chris Pichler: I think so too. Thanks for the invitation. I’m very happy to be doing it.

To get started, what made you fall in love with photo books?

I grew up in a family that was very book oriented. My grandmother was a very well-known author of books for adolescents and we were just all avid readers. So yeah, I grew up with books and I became interested in art and especially photography near the end of high school. And I realized quickly that I actually prefer the way photographs look in books than I do as framed artworks on the walls.

In the mid-80s I was at Arizona State University, which had a very robust artist’s book program at the time, which I looked into a little bit. But I was really turned off because it was more about these very ornate, precious, handmade, one-of-a-kind books with handmade paper and leather and feathers. They were very ’80s. I much preferred something grittier. I was making books of my work, just one-offs using photocopy machines. I learned how to rasterize them all very, very lo-fi and I loved that look. So I think even then, I realized I wanted to be a publisher.

You said that you prefer to see photographs in a book rather than on a wall, but what does a photo book do for photography that an exhibition can’t do?

I think it’s because of a few reasons. One is it’s just so modest. There’s something so modest about a reproduction. And I love beautiful prints. I have some prints by Frederick Sommer, and I get it. I love anybody who can make objects at that level. But I think also it’s a very intimate experience looking at a book. It’s just the person looking at the book and the book itself. Whereas if we’re in a public space looking at pictures, there’s a lot of self-consciousness, I think.

When you encounter a new body of work, what tells you that it might be ready to become a book?

That’s a very almost instantaneous intuitive realization. I don’t ever go out and actively look for projects to publish. And we publish now probably 25 books a year. In all, we’ve published about 800 books over that past 38 years. I’m 60 and I started when I was 22.

That’s a nice lifelong passion!

Yes. I’m very grateful that I’ve been able to do that. And when I look at the books that I’m working on right now, none of them were the result of a search or a hunt for things to publish. Probably 60% of them or more are books by photographers I’ve already published before. Because if I have a good relationship with somebody or a good experience with a photographer, it’s just natural that we’ll continue to work together. So books by Mark Steinmetz, Sage Sohier, Todd Hido, Michael Kenna, there’s many, many by each of these. And then to balance that, it’s pure chance. I’ll be walking along and see something. We don’t accept submissions because we just don’t have the bandwidth for that.

I do try every year to do one or two portfolio reviews because I think it’s important that I’m out there and that I look at work by people who want to show it. Because I remember how it was when I was starting out going to a bookstore and they wouldn’t want to see my books. I know the feeling and both parties have to make an effort. It’s really kind of chance. Sometimes somebody I have a relationship with will share with me work by somebody that they know or work that they’ve seen.

But it’s really important to me to remember that there is work that is so beautiful as an exhibition that wouldn’t function for me as a book. And there’s work that would probably not be a very interesting exhibition that makes a beautiful book. It’s a different medium.

Also, I think with books, there’s a different life span. If there’s an exhibition and nobody goes to it, that’s a disaster. If we publish a book that I really love and it doesn’t sell very well at the beginning, that’s okay. I didn’t publish it to try to sell a whole bunch. I published it because I think it’s important and it’s a big world and I think eventually good books find their homes. So some books I think are probably published before their time. And we’ve published books that sat pretty inactively for a year or two and then something happened and they sell out. So books have a much longer trajectory than do exhibitions, obviously.

For this new prize that we’re launching and you’re going to publish the first book, the prize doesn’t require — or even accept —a finished dummy. Photographers are asked to submit 20 to 30 images and a brief statement. What can you get from that as a publisher? Can 20 to 30 images tell you what you need to know?

Absolutely. Yes. I’m not interested generally in books that have a lot of pictures. Once it’s more than 40 to 50 pictures, I think people get attention span anxiety. I hesitate to pick up a book if it’s got 200 pictures in it because I won’t be able to look at all of them. I lean towards books that have fewer images that make you want more when you’re finished with it. So a lot of our books have 20, 30, 40 images. And so seeing a body of work with 20 to 30 images, that’s kind of a bullseye for me.

You work with some of these superstar photographers who are just always on. It’s always great work. So what makes you willing to take a chance on someone who’s not known yet?

There’s a few reasons for that. First of all, everybody was not known at some point. I try to strike a balance between books by photographers virtually everybody is familiar with and books by photographers that almost nobody is familiar with. And I think those two approaches actually help each other and make the whole catalog stronger. So if we only publish books by superstars, I think it would be kind of soulless. If we only publish books by people who nobody’s heard of, it’d be hard to run a business like that. But I think it’s important that there’s a balance. It’s like a recipe.

How important are the book fairs for you?

We’re going to the San Francisco Book Fair in two weeks and there’ll be hundreds of publishers that I’d never heard of. It’s wonderful. But book fairs are not really any more an important part of our marketing strategy. They used to be. The Frankfurt Book Fair, which I went to from before I started publishing even, that I went to then for the next 20 years, that’s how I met distributors in different countries. That’s how I met key bookstores or key chains in various countries.

Now these days, there are only two fairs I participate in. One is the San Francisco Art Book Fair, and that’s just because it’s such a wonderful fair. It’s such an amazing vibe. It’s so exhibitor-friendly. And it’s a zoo. It’s a madhouse. It’s an exemplary fair.

And the other is a new fair, Show LA, which I actually started along with Giulia Zorzi, who owns Micamera in Milan, probably Europe’s best bookstore, and Keith Cullen, who’s the publisher of Setanta Books in London, who also distributes our books. The three of us founded a photography fair called Show LA. And the initial one was the end of February during Frieze LA this year, just a few months ago. And we borrowed the vibe of the SF Art Book Fair. At least we tried to.

We have a showroom in a building downtown Los Angeles called the REEF, where we’re all working together. Deadbeat Club is involved with several galleries, publishers, artists. And we’re pushing as hard as we can to make that an art building for Los Angeles with the building’s support. And they make it feasible for us to do this. So I feel like we have to do it. If we don’t, I don’t know who else can.

We wanted it to be small in terms of the number of exhibitors. So we had about 25 galleries and about 25 publishers. But it was international. Yeah. I mean, it’s 16,000 square feet, so the booths are huge. We had a lot of space to do this. And of course, we had publishers and galleries from California, but also from Japan and China and Korea and Italy and England. It was wonderful. And the second one will be in December, December 10th to the 13th of this year.

Your books are often remembered as objects as much as publications. And I wonder at what point does the material form become part of the meaning of the book itself?

Part of that grew out of the fact that when I started publishing just out of college in a new country without any money, I had to do a lot of hand work for the books. I couldn’t afford to go to a printer and order that. So I learned how to do very simple binding, just rudimentary. And we started doing things like we published a book by Frederick Sommer called All Children Are Ambassadors. There’s actually three covers and you can open it from either side. It was in German and English. And I had those basically small magazines printed, and then I glued the covers on. And I did that with a number of titles. I had a lot of time at night, I had a lot of energy to do that and it was fun for me. We published a book by Masao Yamamoto that was in a scroll format. It’s literally a scroll so long it’s glued together, maybe 30 feet long. We did a book with Frederick Sommer called The Box, which was literally a set of maybe 50 cards, three by three inches. They were housed in a plexiglass two-piece box. So that’s kind of where the handwork came from, that element. I could make objects. I couldn’t afford mass-produced generic books. But it’s funny right now, I mean over the years and decades actually the company grew. We sell a lot of books. So I can publish a book in any format that makes sense to me, but I find myself being more and more drawn to absolutely simple books, absolutely simple.

We recently did three books that are quite modest and beautiful. In January, we were working on an exhibition of work by Daido Moriyama and Avo Tavitian, two photographers whose work I adore, in Tokyo. And that was for an opening in April. You can’t really publish a standard book starting it in mid-January and having them in April. So we did three very simple books. We did Avo’s, Daido’s, and one by Mark Steinmetz called Lo-Fi Cats. It’s such a beautiful, modest format. So we did those three. The next six are in production right now. I think it’s an important format because, at least for me, it reinforces what my job is as a publisher. And that’s to show photographs in book form and not to overdo the outside of it.

How important is worldwide distribution for a photographer and for a publisher?

For us, it’s really important because we publish a lot of different quantities and formats. We have a series called One Picture Books, and for some of these new Lo-Fi books, we publish 500 or 700 copies. Other titles, we might print 6,000 copies in one print run. And so to sell 500 copies of a book by somebody who’s not really been discovered yet, say, or to sell 6,000 copies by a superstar, we need to go outside the US to do that. So we have very active distribution in France, in Germany, in most of Europe. And China is an important market for us. South Korea is an important market for us. So we need that kind of exposure.

And for a photographer, it’s incredible how well-known somebody can become in another country. Even sometimes they don’t become that well-known in their own country. We’ve published books by Americans who become very, very well known in France or in Japan much more than they do here.

And that opens up the world to them and brings them an audience they wouldn’t have had otherwise.

Right, exactly. Yes.

Is there some kind of advice that you might give to people when they’re thinking about creating a submission? Is there any kind of general advice that might help the jury to appreciate the work?

I am so often pleasantly surprised and even shocked when I see work by somebody who I was not familiar with before and the work is something I never would’ve thought to photograph or maybe it’s a subject I never even considered, but it’s clearly a big part of that person’s life and something they care deeply about. And so whether it’s a book of landscapes or portraits, cityscapes, objects, whatever it is, you can sense if it’s something that they’re really interested in. I’m not interested in trends and in fashions.

I think it’s good for somebody who’s considering to submit work to ask themselves why this work is important to them, why it might be interesting to others. Those are the reasons to publish something — this need to share what you feel is really vital.

I think it’s really important to ask oneself — whether it’s me as a publisher, whether it’s an artist or a photographer who wants a book to exist of their work — why? What’s the point? What do you hope to accomplish?

There is also an important distinction between why do you want to publish a book, and why do you want to make these pictures? And I think the best answer for both of those questions is because I just have to. I don’t know what else I would do with my time.

A Ukrainian artist employs an analog process to create an enduring impression of the war in his hometown, exposing viewers to the day-to-day horrors unfolding in his surroundings.

_Photographs by Vladyslav Krasnoshchok

Book review by Justin Herfst_

[](javascript:;)

Documentation of the War

A Ukrainian artist employs an analog process to create an enduring impression of the war in his hometown, exposing viewers to the day-to-day horrors unfolding in his surroundings.

In our hyperconnected world, we run the risk of war becoming abstract content. Images of the Russian invasion of Ukraine are made and consumed digitally; they are also instantly available. If a battle breaks out, a town is shelled, or a drone strike hits critical infrastructure, a global audience is privy to the images within minutes. Soldiers on the front lines mount GoPros to helmets, tanks, and drones and livestream battles with the enemy. Like most digital content, the horrors of war appear and disappear in an instant—a quick glance by the viewer before scrolling on. Faced with the speed of this media, how can we stay present with the horrors of war?

Perhaps this is where we leave the realm of photojournalism and enter into art. Ukrainian photographer Vladyslav Krasnoshchok’s Documentation of the War immerses the viewer into a collection of images that, in their acute attention to the day-to-day experience of war, brim with emotion. “This book is like a visual novel built over time,” says Krasnoshchok’, one he began photographing in March of 2022 when Russian bombs started falling on his home city of Kharkiv.

From the book “Documentation of the War” © Vladyslav Krasnoshchok[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/vladyslav-krasnoshchok-documentation-of-the-war#)

Krasnoshchok approached the subject of war by breaking down the different ways violence interrupts the everyday life of his surroundings: the destruction of property including bridges, buildings and automobiles; military personnel engaged in the conflict; army equipment such as tanks, drones, and trucks; domestic and wild animals caught in the crosshairs; civilian life under occupation; the various branches of military, such as aviation, artillery, and infantry. He treated each theme as separate directions within one larger body.

From the book “Documentation of the War” © Vladyslav Krasnoshchok[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/vladyslav-krasnoshchok-documentation-of-the-war#)

“I build each photograph as a complete visual form and when many such images come together they create a larger structure—something like a visual novel.” This novel is not a chronological documentary but rather an internal descent. Krasnoshchok explains: “At first the viewer looks at the war from a distance as an observer. Then gradually they are drawn inside the material. And at a certain point the distance disappears—the viewer is no longer looking at the war but is left alone with it.”

From the book “Documentation of the War” © Vladyslav Krasnoshchok[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/vladyslav-krasnoshchok-documentation-of-the-war#)

This shift in position unfolds slowly as the viewer descends into what Krasnoshchok calls ‘geopolitical surrealism,’ a condition that emerges when, in the face of war, reality itself becomes irrational. Kharkiv lies 30 kilometers from the Russian boarder and has been under siege since the beginning of the war. Hundreds of thousands of residents evacuated, many never to return. Krasnoshchok, who lives in his father’s old house, was never going to leave.

From the book “Documentation of the War” © Vladyslav Krasnoshchok[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/vladyslav-krasnoshchok-documentation-of-the-war#)

Krasnoshchok embedded himself with various Ukrainian military units, particularly helicopter pilots. Many became friends and would call him up before heading out on a mission. “When you return again and again you are no longer seen as an outsider,” he says. “You become part of the environment and you begin to work from within.” He photographs soldiers involved in all manner of activity, from travel, to fighting, to resting. Inevitably, a soldier photographed at war one day is photographed deceased another. From his photographs of soldiers emerges the extreme emotions of war, the exhaustion, terror, and tragedy, but also the moments in between—the camaraderie, bravery, and at times even humor. Due to the analog process the photographs look 100 years old, removing the subject matter from the immediate.

From the book “Documentation of the War” © Vladyslav Krasnoshchok[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/vladyslav-krasnoshchok-documentation-of-the-war#)

While out on excursion, Krasnoshchok will shoot a dozen rolls of film, photographing anything that catches his eye. “For me, the most important thing is composition,” he says. “When I see something interesting happening, I try to catch the form. And if I capture the form precisely, it creates the image.” He photographed the war on a variety of film cameras including a Soviet era Horizon Panoramic which he uses to tremendous effect. The wide angle of the photograph seems to cut a strip of reality and freeze it. Panoramic images of destroyed buildings, bombed churches, and tragic scenes of dead soldiers become direct representations of reality as experienced by the artist.

From the book “Documentation of the War” © Vladyslav Krasnoshchok[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/vladyslav-krasnoshchok-documentation-of-the-war#)

Returning from an excursion, Krasnoshchok then develops the film himself and makes prints by hand in the darkroom, often using high contrast developers and a variety of silver gelatin printing techniques to more precisely control the final image. Again, time is the main ingredient; an image is not finished until pulled from the tray of developer. Such a lengthy process removes the print from the immediate, allowing for deeper experience to emerge. “When you capture the form and create an image, it has the strongest impact. The viewer doesn’t just see it—they feel it and begin to empathize with what is inside the image.” True to form, none of the photographs are cropped.

From the book “Documentation of the War” © Vladyslav Krasnoshchok[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/vladyslav-krasnoshchok-documentation-of-the-war#)

Towards the end of Krasnoshchok’s Documentation of the War is a photograph of a man running across an open field with a black horse galloping behind him. The sky is darkened by billowing clouds save for a little light coming from a corner in the horizon. Horse and man are mid stride imbuing both with a fragile emotion. The viewer, having descended into the war, is left with questions. Why are they running? Is this a moment of hope or of tragedy? Are the clouds receding from the light or will they darken to finally consume the last of the day? Such is the experience of Krasnoshchok’s book. Both hope and tragedy, beauty and terror come together in this extraordinary documentation of the war, and in the very end, only questions remain.

Interview

Refusal. Second Fracture

Through images, murals, objects and videos, Rafał Milach’s new exhibition connects propaganda and protest, asking how the region’s political structures might be challenged.

_Photographs by Rafał Milach

Interview by Erik Vroons_

[](javascript:;)

Refusal. Second Fracture

Through images, murals, objects and videos, Rafał Milach’s new exhibition connects propaganda and protest, asking how the region’s political structures might be challenged.

![Image 5: Rafal Milach Rafal Milach](https://www.lensculture.com/rafal-milach)

In a video produced in 2012, a then 13-year-old Belarusian from the town of Oktyabrsky named Xenia Degelko created apatriotic rap songpromoting the Belarusian regime. Hip hop, commonly serving an anti-establishment narrative to empower marginalized minorities, is culturally appropriated here: “I’m an activist of the BRPO (Belarusian Republican Pioneer Organisation), I care about my motherland, I’m ready to support her and to glorify my native land with labor [yeah yeah, yo yo].” From a Western perspective, the song may come across as a ridiculous parody of the genre—Xenia performs all the hand gestures of US-rappers while wearing a traditional school uniform, against the backdrop of a Eurovision-ish decor with folkloristic dancers and flashing neon-lights hyping her message. Nonetheless, the video went viral in Belarus at the time.

Flash forward to 2020. The Polish photographer Rafał Milach is informed that Xenia Degalko, who he had once photographed for his seriesThe Winners, has decided to join the anti-regime rallies in Belarus, following the rigged elections that kept Alexander Lukashenko, ‘the last dictator of Europe,’ in power. Milach, who meanwhile found himself immersed in the anti-establishment activism of his own country, was puzzled and started to rethink his long-term interest in propaganda and protest.

Xenia’s story reveals the fragile mechanisms of political repression: even in a forceful authoritarian machinery, one can detect under-the-radar individualism. This notion became the starting point of Refusal. Second Fracture—currently on view at the Circulo de Bellas Artes in Madrid—in which Milach bridges the fundamentals of his artistic endeavors for the first time. In this interview for LensCulture, Milach speaks to Erik Vroons about the potential of collective practices to challenge existing political structures.

Exhibition view of “Refusal. Second Fracture” at the Circulo de Bellas Artes, Photoespana, 2026 © Rafał Milach[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

Erik Vroons: This PHotoESPAÑA-show echoes themes presented back in 2018, when your exhibition Refusal was nominated for the Deutsche Borse Prize. How does your current exhibition relate to its earlier iteration?

Rafał Milach: Refusal, as I presented it in 2017/18, contained a collection of elements that reflected the affirmation of certain autocratic behaviors as performed in Eastern Europe and post-Soviet states. Thinking back to that set up, there is a junction with what I am now showing in Madrid: The Winners (2010- 2013). The title, Refusal, came from a situation I had with Yuri, a Belarusian ploughman of a collective farm that I wanted to portray in The Winners: a collection of state-organized contest winners, together representing carefully constructed propaganda machinery.

My strategy then was to disguise my real intentions by acting as a ‘propaganda photographer.’ My true purpose was to mirror systemic behaviors that perceive the citizens as instrumental. However, while everything was arranged with his superiors, he simply refused to be photographed. To me, even though this rejection was a small gesture—he was not protesting openly against the system—it was an act of resistance; a fracture in the authoritarian system as I had witnessed it until that moment. This ‘no’ would become a pretext for the whole project.

Belarus / Kryvancy / 21.02.2013 / Kolkhoz administration room where Valeri, the best plowman, refused to be photographed. From the series “The Winners,” 2010–2013 © Rafał Milach[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: In Madrid, The Winners gets a central position again, but with two pictures missing this time, which are then presented on the other side of a constructed wall that you created for this exhibition. Can you explain how this introduces the second fracture?

RM: In 2018, one frame in the grid of winners was left empty—a void representing Yuri’s portrait that I never got to make. Then, a few years later, I found out that around 2020-21, Xenia Degelko, who I also photographed for The Winners, had flipped from being a pro-regime activist to an anti-governmental protester. That was remarkable news to me at the time but it is only now, with an open invitation to propose an exhibition concept for PhotoEspaňa—that Xenia’s repositioning came back into my mind.

Eventually, this led to the idea of juxtaposing two major themes that have been seeping through my work for the past 15 years: systemic propaganda and the gestures of protest. In my understanding, two major themes collide: Xenia switching her ideological position encapsulates the notion of a second fracture in a seemingly continuous and hermetic authoritarian regime, while also serving as a departure point to connect it with my personal involvement in grassroots protest movements in Poland.

Exhibition view of “Refusal. Second Fracture” at the Circulo de Bellas Artes, Photoespana, 2026 © Rafał Milach[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: Speaking of that, can you talk about the contents of the Archive of Public Protest (A-P-P), of which you are a co-initiator?

RM: At its core, the A-P-P is a collective of photographers who aim to create and collect imagery as coming from the various massive street protests that have been organized in Poland since late 2015. We were, until two years ago, ruled by the PiS Party that aggressively defined the political spectrum with their right-wing nationalism and conservatism. Their policies triggered a cycle of street rallies, all with their own specific demands and cries for justice but sharing an overarching concern for violation of democracy and human rights.

Circling back to this exhibition in Madrid, making a connection between the A-P-P and The Winners was honestly never in the orbit of my interest. However, the last year or so—with the PiS Party being outvoted and no longer ruling over Poland from the parliament—allowed for some headspace to reflect on how propaganda and protest, the two main threads in my works, are deeply interwoven. It did not instantly give me a formula for merging these major themes into one presentation but now that this link has been made, it felt inevitable.

From “The Archive of Public Protests,” 2019 © Rafał Milach[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: So, to sum up: you consider propaganda and protest not only running parallel to each other but actually interrelated?

RM: Yes, exactly, but this realization arrived from an organic process defined by the circumstances. This show here in Madrid is not intended to reflect an overview of all my practices; it is more a first gesture of post-conceptualization. I never intended it to be a sequel to Refusal. But, now that I found a micro connection point in the story of Xenia, I am super inspired. Since the inception of the A-P-P, I have presented elements of the protest archive in so many different venues and have had the opportunity to give talks about our collective all over the world but making such an explicit connection with a project from nearly a decade ago is a new experience.

BY. Belarus. Aktyabrsky. 25.03.2013. Xenia Degelko, the president of BRSM pioneer association in Aktyabrsky willage. She is the winner of the “Leader of the Year” contest in the Mogilevsky region. She received a pen engraved with her name from president Lukashenko and dreams of a two floor cottage. From the series “The Winners,” 2010–2013 © Rafał Milach [](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: Looking around, besides your portraits from The Winners, you present mainly non-photographic elements in this exhibition. What do these bring to your photographs?

RM: I felt the urge to be simple and communicative, to move away from the more conceptual manner of documentary photography. The core idea here is that Xenia’s story is further echoed in the space around The Winners wall, where I painted murals depicting activists attending protests across Poland and Ukraine—sourced from A-P-P photographic images.

Throughout the exhibition space, I also plant flags related to the pro-choice movement, the humanitarian crisis at the Polish-Belarusian border, the LGBTQ+ community rallies, or the protests led by Ukrainian and Belarusian diasporas. Each flag stand is accompanied by an edition of the A-P-P Strike Newspaper: a series of protest zines that circulated in more than 44,000 copies—featuring slogans, pictures and protesters’ testimonies. So, in that sense, there is quite a lot of photography included in this show, be it secondary perhaps.

Where I am now, with 20 years of experience working on the discourse between visual arts and politics, things are starting to pile up and make some kind of internal loops. Essentially, my works have started to be in dialogue with each other and the situations that initially occurred chronologically and on their own terms are looping back in a more overarching manner.

Exhibition view of “Refusal. Second Fracture” at the Circulo de Bellas Artes, Photoespana, 2026 © Rafał Milach[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: Let’s bring to the fore one specific element of the installation. In collaboration with fellow-artist and activist Karolina Gembara you had a female protagonist set off a black flare in a gallery space, which was then recorded to become Seeding, a video installation which is also presented in Refusal. Second Fracture. How can we understand this performative act? As an appropriation of what is commonly associated with hooliganism?

RM: I like to apply a wide range of discursive strategies to convey certain ideas. I think using certain gestures from the opposite side can help in demanding attention for your own concerns—and this was well-understood by the women protesting against the introduction of a near-total abortion ban in Poland [The ‘Black Protests’ were a series of massive, women-led demonstrations first erupting in October 2016. The movement gets its name from protesters dressing in black to mourn the loss of reproductive freedoms. Their use of black umbrellas was a symbol of resistance while they also set off black flares, the kind as being widely used by football hooligans and ‘ultras’ groups in the color red to create intimidating atmospheres].

So, yes,Seeding somehow counteracts what extreme hooligans do when they amass in Warsaw during far-right street marches—similar to what they often do inside the football stadiums, by igniting these iconic red flares. We wanted to mirror that with a female protagonist lighting up a black flare, in reference to the ‘Black Protests.’ The appropriation of these vibrant aesthetics is what we aimed to reenact in a gallery setting and we were very lucky that Claudia Cussel, back then a curator at Mai Mano Haz in Budapest, agreed to have us film the performance in the gallery there. We actually proposed such a performance to other venues too but unfortunately none agreed to follow up.

Rafał Milach & Karolina Gembra, “Seeding,” 2018. Courtesy the artists and Jednostka Gallery[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: The works—as objects and what they address—are very forceful, visually, yet also offer spectators to make interconnections on their own terms. Is it fair to say you’re not keen on being overly explanatory, leaning instead on offering strong elements that viewers can draw from?

RM: Everything you see here in Refusal. Second Fracture, is essentially borrowed from various protest strategies with which I became actively engaged for such a long time. I think it all comes down to a desire to find different access paths to a similar subject. Although it is never literally about myself—it is not autobiographical—all these outlets are also very personal. But I also don’t want to lecture anyone or explain the world. My ultimate goal is to use my privileged position as an artist and give a platform to the existence of women’s or LGBTQ+ rights or the aggression against Ukraine and Palestine, among others. However you take it, this is the world we are living in, and that is what I feel I want to bring across. I want it to resonate with everyone with similar concerns.

Exhibition view of “Refusal. Second Fracture” at the Circulo de Bellas Artes, Photoespana, 2026 © Rafał Milach[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: Does showing these murals bring a new dynamic to curating an exhibition?

RM: I’ve actually never exhibited murals on such a scale. With purely photographic presentations, I can prepare my exhibitions in a very detailed way and then it is merely a matter of hanging the works. But when it comes to these large format wall-paintings, I had to set aside a certain amount of time in the days prior to the opening to produce them as large-scale versions of a sketch I made beforehand. So, the process is less controlled than it used to be and that means there is little margin for error. Besides, even though I used to draw before I became a photographer, the mural is not a medium I have become overly familiar with, as I am not really a graffiti artist.

What I have done here in Madrid is both a little bit terrifying and also very exciting as it is a very manual and tactile, or even sensual, process of making. Each mural is also slightly different in the applied technique: the line is different and thus also the gesture varies slightly but you could also say that they developed over time—a photographic depiction made into a drawing, with sampled elements that were in the protests but perhaps not all captured in a single photo, eventually landing here in the exhibition space as a large-scale mural.

Exhibition view of “Refusal. Second Fracture” at the Circulo de Bellas Artes, Photoespana, 2026 © Rafał Milach[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/rafal-milach-refusal-second-fracture#)

EV: Besides appropriation strategies as already discussed, I also sense a growing urge to visualize processes rather than instant situations. Would you agree?

RM: Yes and no. I still believe in the agency of photography, but I am rather interested in how the various outlets I use, be it the camera or the pencil or whatever is in my toolbox, will help me to articulate the matters close to my heart. Photography is still my main medium of expression, but I’m not married to the form: I am married to the message.

My authorship is chronologically about being formed by the transition from Communism to so-called liberal democracy, then becoming resituated within the European Union and the nationalist-conservative defensive mechanism that bounced off from it. Such landmarks for the region that I grew up in are always overarching within a creative ventilation circuit which means that it allows for reconceptualization—as I attempt to do here, by presenting a work from 15 years ago that turns out to be still valid, on a meta level. It’s how I chose it to be but to always adapt myself to tailor-made outlets per venue instead of being on tour with a traveling set can be exhausting. It requires me to respond with finding a unique curatorial formula each time I exhibit.

From “The Archive of Public Protests,” 2019 © Rafał Milach

EV: Given that you are both a founding member of the Sputnik Photos collective and the Archive of Public Protest, generally known to be loyal to the people you work with since the start of your career, how important is the collaborative format for you?

RM: It’s fundamental. If I had to do everything alone I likely would not have the stamina for such complex operations such as The Winners, which actually started as becoming a chapter of an overarching Sputnik group project. Of course, the dynamics vary: in the case of the Archive of Public Protest our mission and shared values are very clear from the get-go, while in Sputnik collective initiatives always need to first arrive from creating a common ground, by discussing the matters of concern before we get to work on a project together.

That’s the scheme but let’s also not forget that Sputnik Photos now exists for 20 years and the A-P-P was only founded around six years ago. They arrive from very different socio-political contexts. Even though the situations in which they both came into being are not the same, these kinds of group dynamics really keep me moving and I think it’s been very rewarding too: the like-mindedness, sharing a geopolitical background. Together, we can approach an issue in a more differentiated way, develop a body of work that is more diverse than when acting on it purely by oneself. That we—myself and my peers—manage to do so, beyond any sort of preconceived formats, is priceless for me.

Either way, I see it as a human responsibility to think and act in terms of solidarity. Alterations in civic society never come for an isolated single action; they arrive from building coalitions, from a combined effort of different entities, and from some kind of endurance within the alliance. That altogether will somehow provoke a message and even though I am very well aware that my artistic involvement is just one of many elements that contributes to it all, I will just keep on offering my share to the demanded shifts in our society.

Editor’s note: Refusal. Second Fracture is on view atPHotoESPAÑAin Madrid until 27 September 2026.

Photography, Still Restless: Les Rencontres d’Arles Festival 2026 Preview

This sprawling, thought-provoking photo festival interrogates the boundary-breaking power of the image as the medium approaches its 200th birthday.

Photographs courtesy Les Rencontres d’Arles

[](javascript:;)

Photography, Still Restless: Les Rencontres d’Arles Festival 2026 Preview

This sprawling, thought-provoking photo festival interrogates the boundary-breaking power of the image as the medium approaches its 200th birthday.

Each summer, the Rencontres d’Arles turns a Provençal city of Roman stones, hot streets, courtyards, churches, and industrial ruins into an argument about images: what they remember, what they invent, what they conceal, and what they can no longer be trusted to prove.

The 2026 edition arrives as photography is nearing its bicentenary—a date usually traced to Nicéphore Niépce’s early camera-made image, View from the Window at Le Gras, made around 1826 or 1827. And an underlying question throughout the wide range of exhibitions is: after two centuries, what can photography still do?

Carlos Idun-Tawiah, Many Reasons to Live Again, 2022. Courtesy of the artist and Galería Alta.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-photography-still-restless-les-rencontres-d-arles-festival-2026-preview#)

One answer comes through Ghana! Dreaming Independence 1957–1976, among the festival’s most enticing anchors. Carlos Idun-Tawiah’s staged, nostalgic, poster image—a young man on a bicycle moving toward us, surrounded by figures who seem to have stepped from memory in their Sunday best—has the buoyancy of a national dream and the knowing theatricality of reconstruction. Bringing together Felicia Abban, James Barnor, Willis E. Bell, Efua T. Sutherland, Paul Strand, Marc Riboud, and younger contemporary artists, the exhibition looks at how a newly independent country pictured itself through books, magazines, stamps, textiles, portraits, and public imagery. Photography here is not just witness; it is nation-building.

![Image 6: Paul Kodjo, Abidjan, 1970s, series Les Soirées dansantes [Dance Parties]. Courtesy of Les Rencontres du Sud and in camera galerie.](https://images.lensculture.com/image/259f5028-8ee7-47ff-2165-de48926d1200/large)

Paul Kodjo, Abidjan, 1970s, series Les Soirées dansantes [Dance Parties]. Courtesy of Les Rencontres du Sud and in camera galerie.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-photography-still-restless-les-rencontres-d-arles-festival-2026-preview#)

Elsewhere in the “Independence” section, Paul Kodjo’s Photoromance captures the promise of Abidjan in the 1970s. Sammy Baloji’s Landscape Lens: A Katangese Crossing takes a more haunted route through family history, colonial archives, extractivism, and the contested terrain of Katanga. Katia Kameli’s The Algerian Novel (A New Chapter) continues her layered meditation on Algeria through postcards, press images, film, and female voices.

Meghann Riepenhoff, Adaptive Radiation #1 (Hanford Reach, Washington, USA, 5.23.2025, River Water, Reference Woman, Reducing Agent), May 23, 2025, series State Shift, 2024–2026, unique dynamic cyanotype Courtesy of the artist.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-photography-still-restless-les-rencontres-d-arles-festival-2026-preview#)

The festival’s “Forms of Life” section may be where Arles feels most sensuous. Meghann Riepenhoff’s Upwelling brings cameraless cyanotypes into contact with water, weather, contamination, and climate instability; her blue-and-white surfaces look less like pictures of nature than weather events persuaded, briefly, to become paper. Lisa Oppenheim’s Monsieur Steichen resurrects Edward Steichen’s floral and textile obsessions through dye-transfer printing and AI—an old master returned as iris, pattern, ghost, and algorithm.

Lisa Oppenheim, Mons Steichen, Version VII, 2024, dye transfer print. Courtesy of the artist and Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York / Los Angeles.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-photography-still-restless-les-rencontres-d-arles-festival-2026-preview#)

Arles also leans into the medium’s current crisis of confidence. We Are Not Alone: Alien Images treats UFO photography as a long prehistory of visual doubt: blurry evidence, belief systems, unstable proof. Clément Cogitore’s Memory Palace folds amateur footage, collective memory, and generative AI into a meditation on what societies choose to remember. Hu Weiyi’s The Inner Darkroom, with film exposed to bodily chemistry, and The Cannibal Image confronts us with pictures like distorted nightmares.

Clément Cogitore, still of Memory Palace, 2026 Courtesy of the artist, Walter Films and ADAGP, Paris.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-photography-still-restless-les-rencontres-d-arles-festival-2026-preview#)

The “Revisits” offer their own pleasures. William Klein, who would have turned 100 this year, is remembered with This Way to Heaven, a reminder that photography can be gloriously unruly. Ming Smith’s Wandering Light delivers blur, spirit, and Black interiority; Harry Gruyaert celebrates saturated color; Martine Barrat restores tenderness and force to photographs made from within marginalized urban communities.

And then there are the younger voices: Jordan Beal, Souleymane Bachir Diaw, Amira Lamti, Mallory Lowe Mpoka, Phan Quang, Charlotte Yonga, and others in the Discovery Award orbit, where truth appears not as a fixed object but something stitched, performed, protected, and approached obliquely.

That may be the promise of Arles this year. Not certainty, but pressure points: independence and inheritance, animals and archives, AI and ancestral memory, beauty and damage. Photography, nearing 200, is not settling into respectability. In Arles, at least, it remains restless.

LensCulture: Distinct Voices Celebrating Pride

In honor of Pride Month, we are highlighting a handful of features that are rooted in identity, queerness, and self expression.

At LensCulture, we’re fortunate to have a global view of contemporary photography, and a community of talented, insightful writers, curators, and interviewers to dig a bit deeper into the various ways people from around the world are using photography to tell stories, express themselves, and share their views of our world.

In honor of Pride Month, we want to highlight a selection of feature articles that do just that. The following projects are raw and honest, centered around identity and expression. We hope you take the time to explore each one and feel inspired to tell your own story.

Rian With Friends. 2017. © Peyton Fulford[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-lensculture-distinct-voices-celebrating-pride#)

Infinite Tenderness

Drawing on the author’s personal experience of growing up in a religious household in the American South, a series that creates an accepting space for America’s queer youth—while offering a visual diary of youth experience across the USA.

Photographs and text by Peyton Fulford

What are you watching? Manipulated NASA image of a film screening at the National Air and Space Museum. The screen has been replaced with an image of two women kissing. © Mackenzie Calle[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-lensculture-distinct-voices-celebrating-pride#)

The Gay Space Agency

The Gay Space Agency imagines an alternative history for NASA, which would allow LGBTQ+ astronauts to fly in space.

Photographs and text by Mackenzie Calle

Ember Claire, 21. “I’m from Indiana. I identify as transfeminine.” © Ernst Coppejans[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-lensculture-distinct-voices-celebrating-pride#)

From the Streets to the Heart — Homeless LGBTQIA+ Youth in New York

A new documentary portrait series focuses on the personal stories of 30 homeless LGBTQIA+ youth and young adults in New York City.

Photographs and stories by Ernst Coppejans

Interview with the photographer by Jim Casper

Hope © Francisco Gomez de Villaboa[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-lensculture-distinct-voices-celebrating-pride#)

Public Matter

In striking and surreal black and white studio scenes, Francisco Gomez de Villaboa invites us to look a little closer at the human body and explore the manifold issues projected upon it.

Photographs by Francisco Gomez de Villaboa

Essay by Magali Duzant

Just Chill © Ugo Woatzi[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lensculture-editors-lensculture-distinct-voices-celebrating-pride#)

Chameleon

Chameleon is a photographic series about hiding and revealing — a metaphor of duality exploring masculinities and spaces beside the heteronormative structure.

Photographs and text by Ugo Woatzi

Florida Boys

Photographs by Josh Aronson

Interview by Magali Duzant

An Alternative Idea of Intimacy

Jeanette Spicer’s evocative portraits of friends and family play with light and space to challenge viewers to rethink intimacy, representation and relationships.

Powerful, defiant portraits that speak to the prevailing strength and presence of LGBTQ people of color in the Netherlands.

Photographs by Dustin Thierry
