In Visible Light: Cinematic Street Photography from Australia

A conversation with Sam Ferris about atmospheric street photography, urban solitude, and how light transforms ordinary city scenes into extraordinary moments.

_Photographs by Sam Ferris

Interview by Sophie Wright_

[](javascript:;)

In Visible Light: Cinematic Street Photography from Australia

A conversation with Sam Ferris about atmospheric street photography, urban solitude, and how light transforms ordinary city scenes into extraordinary moments.

![Image 5: Sam Ferris Sam Ferris](https://www.lensculture.com/samferris)

Sydney’s Central Business District acts as the backdrop to Sam Ferris’ cinematic photographs. When he was a newcomer, fresh from Melbourne, he took to the streets with a camera to orient himself and observe the district at play. In Visible Light is the outcome of over a decade of documenting the flurry of daily activity of its inhabitants as they navigate the difficulties of our current moment. In his dramatic photographs, the city is beautiful and tough, golden light drawing our attention to the hurried activity of its stressed streets and the people coursing through them.

To Ferris, the street has been a tutor. Over the course of many years, the photographer’s gaze on the city and his craft has changed. In photographing his new home, he found belonging, his understanding of the forces shaping the street and Sydney’s post-Olympic identity became more nuanced. In parallel, a mature vision emerged—the kind that welcomes failure and sheds influences in favor of revealing one’s own emotions.

In this interview for LensCulture, Ferris speaks to Sophie Wright about the mystery of the photographic impulse, chasing the surprise of the street and the paradox of being both a participant and an observer.

Foggy Morning, Circular Quay. A quintet of Australian White Ibis fly through the fog and reflected light early on a Winter’s morning at Sydney’s Circular Quay. Due to its increasing presence in the urban environment and its habit of scavenging from human refuse, the species has been colloquially dubbed the ‘bin chicken’ and, in recent years, has become iconic in Australian popular culture. Symbolic of urban Sydney’s encroachment on native habitats, there has been much debate whether to consider these birds a pest or a protected species. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

LC: When did you first take to the street with your camera? What first captivated you about it and what keeps you interested?

Sam Ferris: I came to photography relatively late. I was about 25 and working at a university in Sydney. To clear my head, I started walking everywhere. I liked getting a little bit lost. Eventually I started bringing a camera.

At first I wasn’t photographing people. I was interested in architecture, factories, warehouses and buildings that seemed slightly forgotten or on the verge of disappearing. Thinking about it now, those places probably reflected how I felt at the time. The people came later.

What captivated me then is probably what keeps me interested now. The possibility that something extraordinary can emerge from an ordinary moment. A gesture, an expression, a shaft of light, two strangers passing one another. Things that exist for a fraction of a second and then disappear forever. Fifteen years later, I still haven’t figured it out. Every time I think I understand photography, I make a picture that seems to contradict everything I thought I knew.

Hold Up. The glass surfaces of the shiny, new office buildings at Sydney’s recently developed Barangaroo precinct provide a dramatic setting for street photography. In Aboriginal history, Barangaroo was a powerful Cammeraygal woman of the Eora Nation and a key figure in local Aboriginal culture and community. Commenced in 2011, the 22 hectare precinct consists of towering office buildings, a 270m tall casino and hotel, restaurants, bars, and tourist attractions. According to census data, the population of this area stands at 186. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

SW: How would you characterize your approach and the way it has evolved?

SF: I think early on I was probably chasing photographs that looked like work I’d seen before and admired. Now I’m more interested in photographs that feel like mine.

When I first started, I became fascinated by the visual side of things—composition, layering, color, geometry and especially light. Sydney’s light has a way of exaggerating the everyday. It pours down the streets between buildings, reflects off glass towers and creates these incredible pockets of illumination and shadow. I found myself drawn to those spaces over and over again.

But over time I realized that light wasn’t really the subject. The photographs I care most about now are the ones where the formal elements and the emotional elements align. A photograph might have beautiful light, but if it doesn’t say something about what it feels like to be alive—in that place, at that moment—I lose interest fairly quickly. The older I get, the less interested I am in showing people how clever I am and the more interested I am in showing people how I feel.

Windswept, 2020. The Winter wind whips through a near empty Sydney Opera House precinct, as joggers pass by and Sydney’s few remaining tourists grab a quick selfie in front of the iconic structures in the last minutes of golden, winter light. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

SW: In Visible Light focuses on Sydney’s central business district. What drew you there?

SF: The honest answer is that I didn’t really choose it. I moved to Sydney in 2008 to take up a position at a university. I didn’t know anybody here. I had grown up in the industrial suburbs of western Melbourne and suddenly found myself in this huge city whose pace completely disoriented me.

The CBD became a place I moved through almost every day. Over time, I became fascinated by it. Not because it was the beautiful place I’d seen on postcards—the beaches, the sparkling harbour, the golden light—but because it felt like something bigger in concentrated form. All of the city’s contradiction, its post-Olympics decline seemed to be compressed into a few square kilometres. It’s a city where the cost of living keeps rising along with my sense of anxiety. Both crowded and lonely, aspirational and exhausted.

There are moments where thousands of people are moving through the same space and yet nobody seems connected to anybody else.

Untitled. Corralled on street corners but never connected, commuters begin the journey home. During peak hour, each corner on Sydney’s main thoroughfare of George Street is packed with pedestrians in a mass exodus of the CBD. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

SW: You spent five years working on the project. How did your experience of the area change?

SF: It was closer to 10 years before I felt ready to publish it as a photobook. The city changed, but I probably changed more. When I first arrived in Sydney, I felt overwhelmed by it. I was walking through the CBD trying to understand where I fit within it. Photography became a way of making sense of my place in the city.

Then the more I photographed, the more familiar everything became. I knew where the light would hit at certain times of year. I knew which streets became interesting when it rained. I knew where commuters would emerge from stations and where crowds would bottleneck. It began to feel less intimidating.

At the same time, I started noticing things that I hadn’t seen before. The anxiety. The exhaustion. The pressure people seemed to carry around with them. The subtle ways people navigate public space. I think In Visible Light ended up documenting both journeys simultaneously: my growing familiarity with Sydney and my growing awareness of what life here actually felt like.

Light Rain on George Street. A Summer storm quenches the city and douses commuters during rush hour, after a hot and humid day in Sydney. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

SW: Can you tell me about the title ‘In Visible Light’?

SF: At first people often assumed it was a typo. I quite like that. The title obviously refers to light. Sydney’s light is fundamental to the work. It shapes almost every photograph in the series. But it also comes from a feeling.

When I first moved here, I often felt invisible. Sydney was enormous and indifferent and I felt anonymous within it. Photography became a way of navigating that experience. At the same time, photography itself is a medium obsessed with visibility. It’s supposed to reveal things. The longer I photographed, the more interested I became in ambiguity rather than certainty. In what remains hidden and how little we actually know about the people we pass every day. This play on words title seemed to sit comfortably within that tension.

SW: There’s an interesting dichotomy to devoting yourself to the observation of a place for that long. Often we associate street photography with an ‘outsider’ perspective—but did you feel a sense of belonging emerge after spending that much time on these streets?

SF: Absolutely. Photography allowed me to connect with a city that initially I felt overwhelmed by and eventually learn to see it as home. Without it, I think Sydney would have remained somewhere I lived rather than somewhere I belonged. There’s something peculiar about street photography though; you’re both participant and observer. You’re immersed in public life while standing slightly outside it.

Most of the time I feel almost invisible on the street. You can move in and out of crowds and people barely notice you’re there. It’s a strange feeling, but I quite like it. I think that’s one reason the title resonates with me. Photography allowed me to disappear into the city while also becoming more connected to it. The camera became a bridge rather than a barrier.

Untitled. Inside the newly constructed entrance to Wynyard station on Clarence Street. With the population of Sydney rapidly expanding, Wynyard was upgraded to ease the burden on Sydney’s struggling rail network. At a cost of $100 million AUD, the capacity of the heritage listed station was increased to accommodate 150,000 commuters at any given time. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

SW: What are you looking for when you head out to the street? Can you sketch out what a day’s work looks like for you?

SF: I always struggle with this question because I don’t know if I’m looking for one thing. What I usually say is that it’s there in the rush to or home from the office. It’s there in the stress of trying to have a work-life balance. It’s there in the tedium of the daily commute. It’s there in the packed street corners where masses of people are corralled together but never really connect. It’s there in the brief gestures or expressions that let the facade slip.

Practically speaking, my days are fairly ordinary. I work full-time and have a family, so I’m not wandering around the city for 10 hours a day waiting for inspiration. Most photographs are made in small pockets of time before work, after work or during a commute. Usually I’ll find an interesting scene and wait. Sometimes for five minutes. Sometimes for an hour. Sometimes nothing happens. Failure is the default setting of street photography. You learn to make peace with that.

SW: What do you find to be the most valuable qualities that have helped you navigate the practice of street photography?

Obsession probably helps. My wife would definitely say obsession. I often joke that photography is a passion, an obsession, a sickness, a calling—I don’t really know anymore. But beyond that, I think curiosity is important. Optimism too.

To be a street photographer you have to become a bit of a paradox. You need to remain eternally optimistic while expecting that most of your photographs won’t work. The only expectation I really have when I go out photographing is that I’ll probably fail. If something wonderful happens, that’s a bonus.

I also think honesty matters. The photographs that endure tend to be the ones that say something genuine about the photographer rather than simply showing us what something looked like.

Market Street, 2021. During the beginning of 2021, Sydney returned to relative normality after the Pandemic of 2020. Crowds were back in the CBD, patrolling the shopping stretch of Market and George Streets. In the month of February, the sun finishes its descent at the Darling Harbour end of Market street, creating a spectacular few minutes of light at the close of Summer evenings. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

SW: In your statement you vividly outline the intersecting forces shaping the lives of Sydney’s inhabitants (both non-human and human) from rising conservatism, attacks and riots and urban ecology. Is it important to you that the project captures the specifics of time and place? Did you feel and see these forces play out in the streets or where these conditions you were looking to document?

SF: Very much so. I never wanted the work to be a generic meditation on city life. For me, it’s specifically about Sydney: documenting a city that seemed to peak with the optimism of the 2000 Olympics before gradually losing something of itself, tracing the knife-edge social tensions exposed by the Cronulla riots and still felt today, witnessing the slow erosion of nightlife through the lockout laws, recording a city still carrying the scars of the Martin Place siege and the collective anxiety of the pandemic years. It is about photographing a Sydney where housing has become increasingly unattainable, where status and success are relentlessly pursued, and where many people seem to live with a lingering sense that whatever they have, it might somehow not be enough.

I wasn’t necessarily trying to photograph those things directly. What interested me was how larger social forces reveal themselves in ordinary moments. In body language. In exhaustion. In isolation. In the strange tension that exists between people living shoulder to shoulder while often feeling profoundly alone.

Untitled. Passengers commute on a packed Manly to Circular Quay ferry. A worldwide icon of Sydney, the ‘Freshwater’ ferries are both a rite-of-passage for any visitor to the harbour city and have become quintessential of Sydney life for those who use them for their daily commute. In April 2019, the NSW government announced plans to retire these ferries, sparking public debate and outrage. © Sam Ferris[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/sam-ferris-in-visible-light-cinematic-street-photography-from-australia#)

SW: Did you have any influences for this project? Photographic or non-photographic.

SF: Alex Webb was hugely important for me. I remember borrowing The Suffering of Light from a university library and being completely blown away by it. I still am. The complexity, the layering, the way he uses color and light—it opened my eyes to what photography could do. Joel Meyerowitz was another important discovery. I still remember stumbling across his work in a gallery and feeling something profound click. Closer to home, Trent Parke, Narelle Autio and Jesse Marlow have all been influential. Not just because of the photographs they make, but because they showed me that Australian life could be photographed in a way that felt poetic, strange and emotionally charged.

Outside photography, literature has probably been the biggest influence. I spent years studying and teaching it, and I still think about sequencing photographs the way I think about constructing a narrative.

And then there’s my dad. He’s a painter. Growing up, I’d sit in his studio while he worked. He taught me about perspective, color, composition and form long before I ever thought seriously about photography. At the time I didn’t realize I was learning anything. Looking back now, I suspect I learned how to see before I ever learned how to use a camera.

Editor’s Note: Starting in 2016, Sam Ferris has been acknowledged three times by the LensCulture Street Photography Awards, including winning 2nd Place, Series, in 2021. We are delighted that this year, Sam has agreed to serve on the jury for the LensCulture Street Photography Awards 2026.

Corner of King and George. A woman with a serene expression is struck by a gust of wind at the corner of King and George streets in Sydney’s CBD. During the month of November, there is a 30-minute window in the evening where the light is both direct and reflected, creating a cinematic effect on the street. I have been photographing at this location for roughly five years. © Sam Ferris [](javascript:;)

Outside the Townie. Last light hits the facade of Newtown’s ‘Townie’ Town Hall Hotel. Commuters wait at the traffic lights while patrons line up outside the venue to check in. The hotel has been serving the people of Newtown for over 100 years. © Sam Ferris [](javascript:;)

Reflecting New York - A Brilliant Twist on Street Photography

Using a hand-held mirror, and his very sharp eyes, photographer Stefan Falke allows us to see street scenes from New York we’ve never seen before.

Using a hand held mirror in locations around New York, I invite distant buildings, structures or other nearby scenes into the main photo to create a viewing experience that requires a second look. My goal is to visually loosen up the obvious, to create images that surprise me as much as I hope they will surprise and intrigue the viewer.

L’Artiere Edizioni: Photobooks as Collectible Art Objects

L’Artiere Edizioni’s Gianluca Gamberini talks about collaboration, experimentation and the magic of transforming a body of photographs into a book with a life of its own.

_Interview with Publisher Gianluca Gamberini

Interview by Jim Casper_

[](javascript:;)

L’Artiere Edizioni: Photobooks as Collectible Art Objects

L’Artiere Edizioni’s Gianluca Gamberini talks about collaboration, experimentation and the magic of transforming a body of photographs into a book with a life of its own.

![Image 5: LArtiere Edizioni LArtiere Edizioni](https://www.lensculture.com/l-artiere-edizioni)

L’Artiere Edizioni is a photobook publishing company based in Bologna, Italy. It was founded in 2013 by twin brothers Gianluca and Gianmarco Gamberini. Coming from different, complementary disciplines (Gianluca made movies for 10 years, and Gianmarco had a background in production), they decided to join forces around an artistic medium that they both found fascinating — photobooks.

They got their start when their friend Larry Fink encouraged them to publish the European version of his book, \The Beat\_. They began to develop a series of photobooks, and Larry introduced the brothers to photographer Andrea Modica, whose work they continue to publish today. After a couple years learning the business of publishing and distribution, they continually moved in more and more experimental, conceptual directions for their book designs. Today l’Artiere is highly regarded worldwide as a creator of books that are like collectible works of art themselves.

We’re delighted that Gianluca has agreed to serve on the jury of the first LensCulture Photobook Prize. He spoke with LensCulture’s Jim Casper for this interview. Their conversation has been edited._

Jim Casper: Hi Gianluca. We’re so excited about this new Photobook Prize and really grateful that you’re going to be on the jury. You are known for creating very unique photobooks. Can you tell me a little bit about how you got started, and how you describe your company to people who don’t know it yet?

Gianluca Gamberini: It’s an honor. Thank you.

I think that in our DNA, there are a lot of ideas of experimental things.

After our first two years of publishing excellent traditional books, we wanted really to do something that was more into our idea of a photobook. With Larry’s book and books like the first book with Andrea Modica, we had this chance to start to understand the market and to make the connections with others in the book world. So that was amazing, but it was a little bit limited.

A spread from Larry Fink’s The Beats. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

So Gianmarco and I found that we both really loved this work of Amy Friend — Stardust. She won the Photolucida Award that year. When we saw the work we said, “Oh, I think we could do something different, something unique — in between an artist book and something for a larger public audience.”

And so with Gianmarco, we came up with this idea of interpreting her physical approach to working with archival images in a book. We used the laser to recreate the holes on the page. And then with French binding and very thin paper (like a Bible paper) when you turn the page, you have this impression of light passing through. And that was really like, “Okay! This is what we really like in book.”

From that moment on, we were always trying to treat every book like it was unique. We work with different designers. Every time at the beginning when we decide to work with a photographer, we try to think which designer is the best option for the photographer. And then together with the designer, we work with some idea or concept, and then little by little we create the book.

A fold-out cover for a book by Hitoshi Fugo. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

It sounds like you’re doing something that you’re really passionate about, and it seems like it makes you really happy on a personal level, too.

Very. Very. But I think that every publisher has the same feeling. Otherwise, we probably would do something else.

Yes. Tell me what kind of work seems to fit especially well with L’Artiere?

I think that sometimes it’s difficult to say, but basically we have to fall in love with the work. It has to have a strong sense of empathy for sure. We have to feel the empathy through the image. Sometimes I see that we are very connected also with stories about with connection with family or community. Not always, but that for sure. We really love long-term projects. But this is not always something that you can apply for every book. And also at the end, we need to be able to sell the book to the public. That’s also an important consideration.

A spread from Anders Petersen’s Napoli. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

After 13 years, do you feel you know when a book is going to sell? Do you feel pretty confident?

Gianmarco is better. I’m always confident. He’s better than me, I have to say, in predicting this. But we are 50-50. It’s a democracy, so we try.

It seems like it’s working well. For the LensCulture Photobook Prize, we’re asking photographers to submit 20 to 30 images and a short statement. Is that enough for you as a publisher to gauge whether something would be a good book?

I think that it’s enough to understand or at least to maybe say, “Oh, I want to see more. I want to know more.” It’s a good starting point. Sometimes when I receive an application, I ask photographers to send me a PDF with their own idea of sequence. Even if we will do something completely different, at least we see an intention. And sometimes also I ask if they have already a dummy, send me a video of the dummy even if, again, we will do something completely different. But at least I see something, an intention about it. But I think the 20 image is more than enough to ask. We also have to judge if something that is appropriate for a larger public, and I think the 20 image is great.

And how important is writing to you? A statement, a title, captions, essays — is that a big part of your books or would you say they are more picture and object-oriented?

I think that it is fundamental for a photographer to write about his work. I always ask every photographer to write a little statement about their work. Maybe we will not publish it, but I think it’s very important to have it for both them and for us to better understand the work. We tend to not have curatorial texts. If I have to add something, I prefer to have four or five lines from the photographer at the end at the colophon that is telling in his or her own words. They are photographers, they’re not writers. Nobody’s looking for a Nobel Prize. But I think that that’s the most important text that you can have in a photo book if you need to have it. And some works, of course, are so connected with a text, so of course you need to combine the image with the text.

Tragedia. Photography by Nicola Lo Calzo. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Tell me how you get your books out into the world.

Photo fairs are the greatest for us, even if it’s a lot of work. A fair offers a great way to show your book because at the end we all produce physical objects that you can only appreciate live. And that’s an incredible way of meeting your public. And then of course, as an independent publisher, we sell a lot online on our online store. Also our heroes are bookstores, and especially specialized bookstore around the world. In Europe, I think we have maybe a little bit more of very independent photo bookstores, but in US too, I think. And they are our first target for where to sell our books. We have several distributors: a US distributor and a European distributor, and a little Japanese distributor, who all help us also to sell copies to a larger public.

Our books are objects that become more and more elaborate and precious and the quantities are not so big that I think at one point the people who buy and sell our books are really very passionate about the books.

What does a photo book do that an exhibition or a website or a magazine feature can’t do? What makes a photo book different from those things?

My background is in movies. So for me, this is really a good question. An exhibition is in one moment in time. You create something on a wall, but you give a lot of freedom also to people to interpret it, the narrative. But a book, to me, there is a line and there is a narration. So to me, it’s much more connected to an idea of movie maybe. And also a book stays for a long time. A book doesn’t need electricity to switch on. The magic thing of a book is that when you produce a book, when you publish a book, the book has its own life, and then you never know who will be in touch with the book and how many people will pass the book from one to the other. So that’s also quite magical, I have to say.

Yes. Magical is the word for it. I have favorite books that feel like friends to me. I can take them off my bookshelf and suddenly I’m in a very happy space again. It’s really nice.

That’s exactly the happy space. I think that when you’re not feeling super great, you just spend some time with some photo books, and even if the topics are not maybe the most happy ones, they still give you hope.

Cover of Catholic Girls by Andrea Modica. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Can you give any words of advice to photographers who want to make a photo book?

So first of all is really to do some research. There are many different publishers. It’s a fantastic moment for photo book publisher. We have many, many different ones. And each one of us has really his own particularity. And so I think that I know it’s difficult for a photographer to be very objective about this work, but I think you have to try to see which publisher could be a good fit for you. And maybe, even, don’t be obsessed in having a book that is produced by a publisher because sometime you can do it yourself, and today also is amazing for this. Sometime you can also do a self-publishing book, maybe doing 50 or 100 copies. And I don’t know, it’s just a different way of achieve your objective that is as good as going with a publisher, I think.

I think certainly an advantage of someone publishing a book with you is you have experience, you’re going to put together a book that’s going to be a beautiful object as well as it’s going to treat the photos with respect, but then you’re also going to get it out into the world. It’s not going to sit in someone’s garage because they don’t know how to distribute it. That’s a pretty big part of it, right?

That’s a big part, I have to say. Also, I have to say two other things. I think that not every photography work maybe has to be a book also. Now I think that everyone thinks that his or her work has to be a book. I don’t know. And second of all, I think that — and it’s very important for a photographer, working with a publisher to realize — that it’s really more similar to making a movie. There are many different people working together. Each one has his own idea. Even though photographers are really used to working all by themselves, doing a photo book is teamwork. It is a big collaboration. It’s not easy sometimes to, especially for photographer at their first photo book. It’s difficult sometime if they’re not used to working in team.

What’s your favorite part of the publishing process?

Meeting people. And I think that my favorite part is really when you see a work and you have the capacity to create something new and fresh with the work. That’s really the most magical part. When you see the potential and then you can make it rise above where it is right now.

Often, photographers will say, “Oh, thank you. And thank you to the designer. You allow me to see my work in a different way.” And that’s a great thing, I think.

My Mother Doesn’t Work: Motherhood and Invisible Labor in Pictures

What does it mean to “not work” when your days are consumed by keeping a family and household together? Olga Steinepreis answers with wit, surrealism and a camera.

_Photographs by Olga Steinepreis

Text by Sophie Wright_

[](javascript:;)

My Mother Doesn’t Work: Motherhood and Invisible Labor in Pictures

What does it mean to “not work” when your days are consumed by keeping a family and household together? Olga Steinepreis answers with wit, surrealism and a camera.

“I am officially a housewife,” says Olga Steinepreis introducing her new project. “Saying it out loud still embarrasses me because the word carries a shadow of idleness. Yet there is always work waiting, the kind that keeps a home alive and somehow appears to ‘do itself.’’’ The house in My Mother Doesn’t Work becomes a stage for this invisible cycle of work, full of dirty socks, dishes, erupting mountains of plastic toys. One sole figure is responsible for taming this frenzied environment—Steinepreis, whose body is pictured at work throughout various scenes of domestic labor.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

Photography was an early presence at home while Steinepreis was growing up. Her father was an amateur who developed and printed his own photographs. “As a child, I was fascinated by watching an image slowly appear on a blank sheet of paper in the darkroom,” she recounts. “It felt almost magical.” Years later, the camera’s near-magical power to make things visible remains a defining feature of all of her imaginative projects. Unfolding in parallel with the birth of her first child, her own practice as an artist has allowed her to watch the evolution of her life from a distance, translating her feelings into staged photographs that hold the many—often invisible—facets of motherhood.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

Steinepreis first picked up the camera to still time and document the new person she had brought into the world, before beginning to use it as a compass to navigate her way back to her own identity. “Many experiences of motherhood are difficult to explain with words because they contain contradictions: love and exhaustion, joy and loneliness, fulfilment and the feeling of gradually losing yourself,” she explains. To express this, the artist has developed a visual language steeped in surrealism and absurdity that is deeply rooted in this myriad of emotions she experiences in everyday reality.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

Both a self-portrait and a character that is being performed, the figure animating Steinepreis’ images morphs across projects. In another series, I’ve had a dream…, the artist is a shapeshifting being, stretched in different directions with extra arms and heads. She multiples herself, different selves staring each other down. In My Mother Doesn’t Work, it is things that multiply, drowning out the faceless body—invisible, unrecognized chores that rack up over time amassing to excess.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

“Usually, my projects begin with something that refuses to leave me alone. It can be a sentence I overhear, an everyday situation, a feeling of discomfort, or a contradiction I don’t quite understand,” Steinepreis says. The earworm of My Mother Doesn’t Work was a snippet of conversation that she overheard during a conversation between her son and his friend. When asked what his mother did for a living, the artist’s son replied: “My mom doesn’t work. Well, she cooks, keeps the house clean, but she hasn’t got a real job.” The innocent remark returned to her again and again as she performed her daily chores at home.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

“One day, while sorting a pile of laundry before putting it into the washing machine, I felt the urge to set up my camera and lights and took a photograph,” she explains. “That image never became part of the final series, but it marked the beginning of the project. It gave me the visual language I wanted to continue exploring and opened up a conversation I felt compelled to have through photography.”

In elaborately constructed scenes, Steinepreis’ frantic body disappears into the environment she has been tasked with keeping in working order. During the work process, artistic and domestic labor meet. “Before I can even begin shooting, I often have to prepare for the day in a very practical way. I cook meals in advance and try to free myself from as many household responsibilities as possible,” she says. “When I finally get to realize the vision, it becomes a very physical undertaking. I move furniture, rearrange objects, layer the scene with deliberate care, and craft the lighting to support the mood. It’s like staging a small theatre set.” Both humorous and upsetting, the dramatized version of everyday life that gets played here feels closer to reality than the pristine narrative of motherhood that dominates social media.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

“Will I ever live up to this ideal? Who set this standard in the first place? The issue isn’t that these bright, beautiful moments exist—they absolutely do. The problem arises when they become the only acceptable narrative of motherhood,” the artist ponders. “There’s so little room for honest conversations about the exhaustion, the frustration, the invisible labor, or the slow erosion of one’s own needs beneath the weight of everyone else’s demands. A woman’s time, energy, and attention get reoriented entirely around others. Even small, everyday choices—what to cook, when to rest, how to spend her time—are made with everyone else in mind. Gradually, she can start to fade out of her own story.”

Across the projects that make up her body of work, Steinepreis goes beyond writing her way back into her own story to explore a more collective narrative. “I am not interested in portraying motherhood only as struggle or sacrifice, just as I am not interested in presenting it as endless joy.”
